title: 4 Ways to Screw Up (and Fix) In-class Arguments
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: After a lunchtime student debate about video game consoles fell apart, Stuart uses it to catalog four ways in-class arguments go wrong and how to fix them. Dominant talkers need structured management such as speak-once-before-twice rules, note cards, and timers. Disrespect must be addressed because the best debaters represent opponents so accurately that the opponents would accept the summary. Crosstalk is handled with a firm rule or a scheduled cross-examination segment. Finally, skimping on preparation, especially strategy time, undermines the exercise. He closes by treating even a failed debate as a lesson, and links the points to the speaking, listening, and research standards.
points: Debate management is framed as classroom culture work: dominators, disrespect, and crosstalk each need a specific, consistent response.
Structural rules like speaking once before twice, timed turns, and note-card cold-calling keep arguments inclusive.
Teaching students to summarize an opponent's case fairly makes arguments both more civil and more compelling.
A sample schedule with research, strategy planning, arguments, and cross-examination shows how preparation time fixes a chaotic debate.
quotes: Every class has its dominators — the kids who love arguing or who are great at it or who love to win or who simply love to talk. These kids are great to have, but they require special management if a truly argumentative classroom is to form.

This was so much fun. I applaud my students for taking it upon themselves to carry out an intellectual debate during their lunch time (I couldn’t help but be reminded of one of my favorite essays of all time: Gerald Graff’s “Hidden Intellectualism,” which is found in the back of They Say, I Say).

At the start of the year, I found that students assumed the way to win in a debate was to make your opponents appear as stupid as possible. Now, don’t get me wrong: a great debater knows how to systematically dismantle any opponents argument.

However, in the process, a great debater is also respectful of her opponent, making sure to accurately represent the opposing side. In fact, I think the most compelling arguments are those that summarize their opponent’s arguments in a manner that the opponents themselves would summarize them.
